newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Intel says all chips to have MMX by early 1998.
newsitem.headline: Intel says all chips to have MMX by early 1998.

text.p: U.S. microchip giant Intel Corp, hoping to tighten its grip on the world market, said on Friday that all of its flagship Pentium chips would have MMX multimedia enhancement technology by the second quarter of 1998.
Intel, which analysts say commands 80 percent of the global microprocessor market, said MMX also would be standard in the second generation of Pentium chips due for release in May.
"By the beginning of next year (1998) MMX technology will be included in virtually 100 percent of all our chips," the company's Asia-Pacific vice president, Sean Maloney, told reporters.
"By the second quarter of 1998 absolutely 100 percent of all our chips will have MMX."
Intel launched the MMX chip, which supports voice and audio data processing and other multimedia functions, in January.
Analysts said MMX has effectively defined a new standard for the industry, as computer and peripheral makers have scrambled to accommodate the technology to meet strong market demand.
A March industry study by the U.S. research group Computer Intelligence showed that the MMX Pentium had already grabbed a 27 percent share of desktop units sold in January.
Intel on Friday affirmed it would introduce a new generation of chips called Pentium 2 in May.
Maloney said Intel planned to detail the Pentium 2 launch for manufacturers at a May 5 technology forum for Taiwan's huge computer industry.
"We have been working with Taiwanese computer designers for a very long time now on Pentium 2, and everything looks very healthy," Maloney said.
The Pentium 2 is expected to boast clock speeds of 400 megahertz and above -- doubling the 200 MHz of the fastest current Pentiums.

While Intel has billed MMX as a great advance for multimedia computers, it acknowledged the technology would not replace sound cards, graphics accelerators and other multimedia auxiliaries as some early promoters had predicted.
"The MMX cannot act as a replacement for something like the sound card. Rather, it can only enhance the quality offered by the sound card," said Intel Taiwan market manager Joseph Lin.
"Many people have this misconception that you can just plug in an MMX card and the computer automatically turns into a stereo or a video player. That is not true."
